newsitem.title: USA: Fla. drops Unisys as administrator.
newsitem.headline: Fla. drops Unisys as administrator.

text.p: Florida and Unisys Corp. have agreed to end the company's contract to administer the state's health insurance plan two years ahead of schedule after allegations of mismanagement, state officials said Thursday.

Without laying blame, the state said the contract, affecting 215,000 state workers covered under Florida's self-insurance fund, will end on Dec. 31. They said they hope to have a new administrator in place by Jan. 1.
The announcement capped a rocky relationship between the state and Unisys, which in late 1995 was awarded the contract for administering Florida's insurance programme.

Unisys beat Blue Cross/Blue Shield of Florida Inc. with an $86.6 million bid for the contract, which was for four years with additional four one-year renewals. Blue Cross, which had held the contract for 17 years, had bid $102.2 million.
Shortly after Unisys took over, complaints began pouring in from customers whose claims were not being paid.

An audit of the company in June 1996 revealed that Florida taxpayers may be forced to pay an additional $21 million a year for coverage because Unisys was not receiving the same discounts that Blue Cross had enjoyed.
Under the agreement to end the pact, Unisys will be paid for the portion of work completed and will assist the state in making the transition to a new administrator.
State officials say they have begun talks with Aetna Inc., CIGNA Corp., Blue Cross/Blue Shield of Florida, Humana Inc. and other providers.

"Our state workers, their families and our retirees depend on the security provided by quality, affordable health care," Florida Governor Lawton Chiles said in a statement. "We must take every possible step to ensure our state workers have the highest faith in their health care providers."
A spokesman said Unisys, which is based in Pennsylvania, agreed with the state's decision to end the contract and will step out of the self-insurance administration market.

"Obviously we have had our problems and have put a tremendous amount of money and time trying to solve them," spokesman Peter Hynes said. "We have made progress, but we agree with the state's decision to go this way with its health insurance business."
